claim: Greater than 90% of corticospinal projections project to the contralateral spinal cord.
source: Anatomically, greater than 90% of corticospinal projections project to the contralateral spinal cord (Dum and Strick, 1996; Brösamle and Schwab, 1997; Lacroix et al., 2004; Rosenzweig et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Most of the 10% of corticospinal projections that project ipsilaterally bifurcate and synapse bilaterally, with few thought to synapse purely onto ipsilateral targets.
source: Most of the 10% that project ipsilaterally bifurcate and synapse bilaterally, with few thought to synapse purely onto ipsilateral targets (Rosenzweig et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rosenzweig et al., 2009.

claim: There are many monosynaptic projections from M1 to contralateral limb motoneurons.
source: While there are many monosynaptic projections from M1 to contralateral limb motoneurons (Bennett and Lemon, 1996; Bennett and Lemon, 1996; McKiernan et al., 1998; Smith and Fetz, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There are no monosynaptic projections from M1 to ipsilateral motoneurons.
source: there are no monosynaptic projections from M1 to ipsilateral motoneurons (Soteropoulos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Soteropoulos et al., 2011.

claim: Stimulation in M1 largely produces contralateral movements and occasionally bilateral movements.
source: Stimulation in M1 largely produces contralateral movements and occasionally bilateral movements (Montgomery et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Montgomery et al., 2013.

claim: Inactivation of ipsilateral motor cortex has minimal effects on ipsilateral hand movements.
source: Lastly, inactivation of ipsilateral motor cortex has minimal effects on ipsilateral hand movements (Nishimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nishimura et al., 2007.

claim: An early study suggested M1 was largely insensitive to ipsilateral movement.
source: An early study suggested M1 was largely insensitive to ipsilateral movement (Tanji et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tanji et al., 1988.

claim: Several subsequent studies highlight substantial M1 activity during ipsilateral movements.
source: However, several subsequent studies highlight substantial M1 activity during ipsilateral movements (Donchin et al., 1998; Kermadi et al., 1998; Cisek et al., 2003; Bundy and Leuthardt, 2019; Willett et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: 46% of neurons in macaque M1 responded to both ipsilateral and contralateral hand movements.
source: They found 46% of neurons responded to both hand movements, whereas 34% of neurons responded to only contralateral movements and 19% responded to only ipsilateral movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donchin et al. (2002) in the preceding sentence.

claim: 34% of neurons in macaque M1 responded to only contralateral hand movements.
source: They found 46% of neurons responded to both hand movements, whereas 34% of neurons responded to only contralateral movements and 19% responded to only ipsilateral movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donchin et al. (2002) in the preceding sentence.

claim: 19% of neurons in macaque M1 responded to only ipsilateral hand movements.
source: They found 46% of neurons responded to both hand movements, whereas 34% of neurons responded to only contralateral movements and 19% responded to only ipsilateral movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donchin et al. (2002) in the preceding sentence.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) revealed considerable motor cortical activity related to ipsilateral movements.
source: As well, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) revealed considerable motor cortical activity related to ipsilateral movements (Cramer et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2003; Gallivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Areas in motor cortex associated with an ipsilateral digit overlapped with its representation for the corresponding contralateral digit.
source: In particular, Diedrichsen et al. (2013) found areas in motor cortex associated with an ipsilateral digit overlapped with its representation for the corresponding contralateral digit.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diedrichsen et al. (2013).

claim: M1 activity unrelated to downstream motor targets can be segregated from activity related to the downstream motor output.
source: Our results show that M1 activity unrelated to downstream motor targets can be segregated from activity related to the downstream motor output.
evidence: This claim is presented as a main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and analyses described in the manuscript.

claim: M1 activity can cancel out at spinal circuits.
source: One hypothesis is that this M1 activity cancels out at spinal circuits (Druckmann and Chklovskii, 2012; Kaufman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Motor cortex can perform computations necessary for planning an upcoming movement without causing movement by using null patterns.
source: This strategy can allow motor cortex to perform computations necessary for planning an upcoming movement without causing movement (Churchland et al., 2012; Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rapid visual feedback of the hand may be isolated in subspaces orthogonal to the subspaces used for the subsequent motor correction.
source: Similarly, rapid visual feedback of the hand may be isolated in subspaces orthogonal to the subspaces used for the subsequent motor correction (Stavisky et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stavisky et al., 2017.

claim: Ipsilateral activity occupies subspaces that are orthogonal to contralateral activity.
source: Thus, this hypothesis predicts that ipsilateral activity occupies subspaces that are orthogonal to contralateral activity.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis prediction based on the null space theory.

claim: M1 responds to proprioceptive feedback.
source: Several studies have shown M1 responds to proprioceptive feedback (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Wolpaw, 1980; Chapman et al., 1984; Pruszynski et al., 2011; Takei et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: M1 represents loads applied to the contralateral limb.
source: Several studies have shown M1 responds to proprioceptive feedback (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Wolpaw, 1980; Chapman et al., 1984; Pruszynski et al., 2011; Takei et al., 2018) and represents loads applied to the contralateral limb (Cabel et al., 2001; Herter et al., 2009; Omrani et al., 2014; Pruszynski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ~55% of neurons in M1 were active when loads were applied to the contralateral and ipsilateral limbs.
source: We found ~55% of neurons were active when loads were applied to the contralateral and ipsilateral limbs.
evidence: This claim is presented as a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: Contralateral loads tended to evoke neural responses that were twice as large as responses for ipsilateral loads.
source: However, contralateral loads tended to evoke neural responses that were twice as large as responses for ipsilateral loads.
evidence: This claim is presented as a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: Contralateral loads evoked changes in neural activity ~10 ms earlier than ipsilateral loads.
source: Furthermore, contralateral loads evoked changes in neural activity ~10 ms earlier than ipsilateral loads.
evidence: This claim is presented as a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: Contralateral activity occupied subspaces that were orthogonal to the ipsilateral activity.
source: Lastly, we found contralateral activity occupied subspaces that were orthogonal to the ipsilateral activity suggesting a mechanism on how motor cortex can sequester the ipsilateral activity without causing contralateral movement.
evidence: This claim is presented as a finding from the current study's data analysis.

claim: The load caused Monkey P's perturbed hand to deviate ~1 cm before the monkey returned the hand to the target when contralateral loads were applied.
source: The load caused the perturbed hand to deviate ~1 cm before the monkey returned the hand to the target.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Changes to the speed of the unperturbed limb appeared to start in <100 ms when contralateral loads were applied.
source: In the unperturbed limb (left limb), we observed much smaller hand motion and changes to the speed appeared to start in <100 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When ipsilateral loads were applied, the perturbed limb deviated ~2 cm from the start position.
source: When loads were applied to the ipsilateral limb only, the perturbed limb deviated ~2 cm from the start position while the unperturbed limb showed minimal hand motion (Figure 2C–D, supplementary 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The unperturbed limb showed minimal hand motion when ipsilateral loads were applied.
source: When loads were applied to the ipsilateral limb only, the perturbed limb deviated ~2 cm from the start position while the unperturbed limb showed minimal hand motion (Figure 2C–D, supplementary 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Hand speeds were an order of magnitude larger when loads were directly applied to the limb versus loads applied to the opposite limb.
source: Hand speeds were an order of magnitude larger when loads were directly applied to the limb versus loads applied to the opposite limb (ratio between perturbed and unperturbed motion: right limb Monkey p=15, Monkey M = 9.7; left limb: Monkey p=10, Monkey M = 8.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of kinematic data from both monkeys.

claim: A clear increase in muscle activity can be observed in <50 ms when the limb was perturbed.
source: A clear increase in muscle activity can be observed in <50 ms when the limb was perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There was little change in muscle activity when the opposite limb was perturbed.
source: In contrast, there was little change in muscle activity when the opposite limb was perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A significant increase in RMS muscle activity from baseline was detected when the limb was perturbed (paired t-test t(4) = 11.7 p<0.001).
source: A significant increase from baseline was detected when the limb was perturbed (paired t-test t(4) = 11.7 p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: No significant change in RMS muscle activity was detected when the opposite limb was perturbed (t(4) = 0.8 p=0.48).
source: while no significant change was detected when the opposite limb was perturbed (t(4) = 0.8 p=0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: Four of five muscle samples had a significant interaction effect between epoch and load combination when the limb was perturbed.
source: When the limb was perturbed, four of five muscle samples had a significant interaction effect between epoch and load combination (F(7,176)=5.3, p<0.001, F(7,160)=15.4 p<0.001, F(7,96)=11.4, p<0.001, F(7,96)=2.3 p=0.04)
evidence: This claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: One muscle sample exhibited a significant main effect of epoch when the limb was perturbed (F(1,160), p=0.006).
source: while the remaining muscle exhibited a significant main effect of epoch (F(1,160), p=0.006).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: No muscle samples were significant when the opposite limb was perturbed.
source: No muscle samples were significant when the opposite limb was perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: 92 neurons were recorded from M1 in Monkey P.
source: From Monkeys P and M, we recorded 92 and 130 neurons from M1, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of neurons recorded.

claim: 130 neurons were recorded from M1 in Monkey M.
source: From Monkeys P and M, we recorded 92 and 130 neurons from M1, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of neurons recorded.

claim: For Monkey P, 90 neurons were load-sensitive.
source: For Monkey P/M we found 90/91 neurons had either a significant main effect of epoch or interaction effects with epoch, indicating that they were load sensitive (thus referred to as 'load-sensitive' neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by three-way ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: For Monkey M, 91 neurons were load-sensitive.
source: For Monkey P/M we found 90/91 neurons had either a significant main effect of epoch or interaction effects with epoch, indicating that they were load sensitive (thus referred to as 'load-sensitive' neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by three-way ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 48% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had significant fits for the ipsilateral and contralateral loads.
source: During the perturbation epoch, for Monkey P/M we found 48/60% of load-sensitive neurons had significant fits for the ipsilateral and contralateral loads
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 60% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had significant fits for the ipsilateral and contralateral loads.
source: During the perturbation epoch, for Monkey P/M we found 48/60% of load-sensitive neurons had significant fits for the ipsilateral and contralateral loads
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 11% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only.
source: whereas 11/11% of neurons had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 11% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only.
source: whereas 11/11% of neurons had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 39% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
source: and 39/18% of neurons had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the perturbation epoch, 18% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
source: and 39/18% of neurons had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between ipsilateral and contralateral fit probability values for Monkey P (r = −0.1).
source: We found no significant correlation for Monkey P (Pearson's correlation coefficient r = −0.1)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a moderate positive correlation between ipsilateral and contralateral fit probability values for Monkey M (r = 0.4).
source: and a moderate positive correlation for Monkey M (r = 0.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 51% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had significant fits for both contexts.
source: During the steady-state epoch (last 1000 ms of trial), for Monkey P/M we found 51/53% of neurons had significant fits for both contexts
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 53% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had significant fits for both contexts.
source: During the steady-state epoch (last 1000 ms of trial), for Monkey P/M we found 51/53% of neurons had significant fits for both contexts
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 16% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only.
source: whereas 16/13% of neurons had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 13% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only.
source: whereas 16/13% of neurons had a significant fit for ipsilateral loads only
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 30% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey P had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
source: and 30/26% of neurons had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, 26% of load-sensitive neurons in Monkey M had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
source: and 30/26% of neurons had a significant fit for contralateral loads only.
evidence: This claim is supported by planar fit analysis of neural data.

claim: There was no correlation between ipsilateral and contralateral fit probability values during the steady-state epoch for Monkey P (r = −0.1).
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D shows no correlation between probability values for the ipsilateral and contralateral fits for either monkey (Monkey P/M: r = −0.1/0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no correlation between ipsilateral and contralateral fit probability values during the steady-state epoch for Monkey M (r = 0.02).
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D shows no correlation between probability values for the ipsilateral and contralateral fits for either monkey (Monkey P/M: r = −0.1/0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For Monkey P, ipsilateral preferred loads showed significant bimodal distributions in both the perturbation and steady-state epochs (p<0.001 and p<0.01, respectively).
source: For Monkeys P and A, we found significant bimodal distributions in both epochs (bootstrap from uniform null distribution: perturbation epoch Monkey P: p<0.001; Monkey M: p<0.001, steady-state Monkey P: p<0.01; Monkey M: p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For Monkey M, ipsilateral preferred loads showed significant bimodal distributions in both the perturbation and steady-state epochs (p<0.001 and p<0.01, respectively).
source: For Monkeys P and A, we found significant bimodal distributions in both epochs (bootstrap from uniform null distribution: perturbation epoch Monkey P: p<0.001; Monkey M: p<0.001, steady-state Monkey P: p<0.01; Monkey M: p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: For both monkeys, the major axis of the bimodal distributions for ipsilateral loads resided in the quadrants for combined shoulder extension/flexion and elbow flexion/extension.
source: For both monkeys, the major axis of the bimodal distributions resided in the quadrants for combined shoulder extension/flexion and elbow flexion/extension (Figure 4A,F quadrants 2 and 4, red line).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of preferred load distributions shown in Figure 4A,F.

claim: The difference between a neuron's preferred load during the perturbation and steady-state epochs for ipsilateral loads revealed a significant unimodal distribution with a major axis near zero for both monkeys (p<0.001).
source: Calculating the difference between a neuron's preferred load during the perturbation and steady-state epochs revealed a significant unimodal distribution with a major axis near zero (Figure 4D,I, bootstrap from uniform null distribution, p<0.001, both monkeys).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D,I.

claim: For contralateral loads, significant bimodal distributions were found for the perturbation and steady-state epochs in Monkey P (p<0.05 and p<0.01, respectively).
source: For the contralateral loads, we found significant bimodal distributions for the perturbation and steady-state (Figure 4B,G: perturbation epoch Monkey P: p<0.05; Monkey M: p<0.001, steady-state Monkey P: p<0.01; Monkey M: p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For contralateral loads, significant bimodal distributions were found for the perturbation and steady-state epochs in Monkey M (p<0.001 and p<0.05, respectively).
source: For the contralateral loads, we found significant bimodal distributions for the perturbation and steady-state (Figure 4B,G: perturbation epoch Monkey P: p<0.05; Monkey M: p<0.001, steady-state Monkey P: p<0.01; Monkey M: p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The difference between a neuron's preferred load during the perturbation and steady-state epochs for contralateral loads revealed significant unimodal distributions with a major axis near zero for both monkeys (p<0.001).
source: Calculating the difference between a neuron's preferred load during the perturbation and steady-state epochs also revealed significant unimodal distributions with a major axis near zero for both monkeys (Figure 4E,J, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E,J.

claim: For Monkey P, the distribution of differences between each neuron's preferred load between the ipsilateral and contralateral limb showed no unimodal structure for either epoch (p=0.2).
source: For Monkey P, we found the distribution showed no unimodal structure for either epoch (Figure 4C, perturbation epoch and steady-state, p=0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For Monkey M, the distribution of differences between each neuron's preferred load between the ipsilateral and contralateral limb showed a unimodal distribution with a major axis near 180° for both epochs (p<0.01).
source: For Monkey M we found a unimodal distribution with a major axis near 180° for both epochs (Figure 4H, perturbation and steady-state epochs, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Directional tuning is more similar across epochs than across the limbs.
source: These results suggest that directional tuning is more similar across epochs than across the limbs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of preferred load distributions across epochs versus across limbs.

claim: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads than ipsilateral loads during the perturbation epoch.
source: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads (median of all neurons Monkey P: 39 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 24 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 16 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 13 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 5A,E.

claim: The median firing rate for contralateral loads during the perturbation epoch was 39 Hz/Nm for Monkey P.
source: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads (median of all neurons Monkey P: 39 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 24 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 16 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 13 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the median firing rate from the data.

claim: The median firing rate for contralateral loads during the perturbation epoch was 24 Hz/Nm for Monkey M.
source: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads (median of all neurons Monkey P: 39 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 24 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 16 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 13 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the median firing rate from the data.

claim: The median firing rate for ipsilateral loads during the perturbation epoch was 16 Hz/Nm for Monkey P.
source: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads (median of all neurons Monkey P: 39 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 24 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 16 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 13 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the median firing rate from the data.

claim: The median firing rate for ipsilateral loads during the perturbation epoch was 13 Hz/Nm for Monkey M.
source: More than 70% of the neurons had a larger firing rate for contralateral loads (median of all neurons Monkey P: 39 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 24 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 16 Hz/Nm; Monkey M: 13 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the median firing rate from the data.

claim: The difference between each neuron's contralateral and ipsilateral firing rate during the perturbation epoch yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for Monkey P (z = 5.1 p<0.001).
source: The difference between each neuron's contralateral and ipsilateral firing rate yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for both monkeys (Figure 5B F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 5.1 p<0.001, Monkey M: z = 5 p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The difference between each neuron's contralateral and ipsilateral firing rate during the perturbation epoch yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for Monkey M (z = 5 p<0.001).
source: The difference between each neuron's contralateral and ipsilateral firing rate yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for both monkeys (Figure 5B F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 5.1 p<0.001, Monkey M: z = 5 p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 5F.

claim: During the steady-state epoch, contralateral loads evoked larger firing rates (Monkey P: 25 Hz/Nm, Monkey M: 16 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 10 Hz/Nm, Monkey M: 10 Hz/Nm).
source: Similarly, during the steady-state epoch, we found the contralateral loads evoked larger firing rates (Figure 5C G, note scales are smaller than for 6A and E; Monkey P: 25 Hz/Nm, Monkey M: 16 Hz/Nm) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 10 Hz/Nm, Monkey M: 10 Hz/Nm).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of firing rates shown in Figure 5C,G.

claim: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral magnitudes during the steady-state epoch yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for Monkey P (z = 5.9 p<0.001).
source: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral magnitudes yield a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for both monkeys (Figure 5D H, Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 5.9 p<0.001, Monkey M: z = 4.6 p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral magnitudes during the steady-state epoch yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for Monkey M (z = 4.6 p<0.001).
source: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral magnitudes yield a distribution that was significantly shifted to the right for both monkeys (Figure 5D H, Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 5.9 p<0.001, Monkey M: z = 4.6 p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Approximately a quarter of the neurons displayed larger responses for the ipsilateral limb across epochs and monkeys.
source: However, approximately a quarter of the neurons displayed larger responses for the ipsilateral limb across epochs and monkeys.
evidence: This is an inference from the firing rate comparison data.

claim: For Monkey P, responses for the contralateral loads started at 28 ms and for ipsilateral loads at 39 ms.
source: For Monkey P, responses for the contralateral and ipsilateral loads started at 28 ms and 39 ms, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by onset analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For Monkey M, the response for the contralateral loads started at 51 ms.
source: For Monkey M, the response for the contralateral loads started later than for Monkey P at 51 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by onset analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For Monkey M, the response for the ipsilateral loads was detected at 57 ms.
source: However, the response for the ipsilateral loads was still detected later at 57 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by onset analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: More than 70% of neurons had an onset earlier for contralateral loads (median onset Monkey P: 68 ms, Monkey M: 79 ms) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 81 ms, Monkey M: 117 ms).
source: From this population more than 70% of neurons had an onset earlier for contralateral (median onset Monkey P: 68 ms, Monkey M: 79 ms) than ipsilateral loads (Monkey P: 81 ms, Monkey M: 117 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by onset comparison analysis shown in Figure 6B,F.

claim: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral onsets yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the left for Monkey P (z = 2.7 p<0.01).
source: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral onsets yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the left for both monkeys (Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 2.7 p<0.01, Monkey M: z = 4 p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral onsets yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the left for Monkey M (z = 4 p<0.001).
source: The difference between contralateral and ipsilateral onsets yielded a distribution that was significantly shifted to the left for both monkeys (Wilcoxon signed-rank test Monkey P: z = 2.7 p<0.01, Monkey M: z = 4 p<0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test shown in Figure 6G.

claim: 30% of neurons had response times that were earlier for the ipsilateral limb.
source: However, 30% of neurons had response times that were earlier for the ipsilateral limb.
evidence: This is an inference from the onset comparison data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between magnitude and onset timing for the contralateral activity in both monkeys (Monkey P: r = −0.08, Monkey M: r = 0.13).
source: For both monkeys, we found no significant correlations between magnitude and onset timing for the contralateral (Pearson's correlation coefficient: Monkey P: r = −0.08, Monkey M: r = 0.13)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of magnitude and onset timing.

claim: There was no significant correlation between magnitude and onset timing for the ipsilateral activity in both monkeys (Monkey P: r = 0.12, Monkey M: r = 0.004).
source: and ipsilateral activity (Monkey P: r = 0.12, Monkey M: r = 0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of magnitude and onset timing.

claim: There was no apparent relationship between the magnitude ratio and onset differences for Monkey P (r = −0.08) and Monkey M (r = −0.07).
source: In both monkeys, we saw no apparent relationship between the magnitude and onsets (Monkey P/M: −0.08 /- 0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D,H.

claim: For a subset of neurons with absolute magnitude difference <20 Hz, contralateral loads tended to evoke earlier responses than ipsilateral loads for Monkey M (z = 2.8 p<0.01).
source: For Monkey M, we found a significant leftward shift in the distribution of onset differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 2.8 p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test on a subset of neurons shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: For a subset of neurons with absolute magnitude difference <20 Hz, there was a leftward shift in the distribution of onset differences for Monkey P, but it was not significant (z = 1.4 p=0.17).
source: For Monkey P we also found a leftward shift in the distribution, however it was not significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, z = 1.4 p=0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by Wilcoxon signed-rank test on a subset of neurons shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The earlier onset times for the contralateral loads were not simply due to larger changes in activity.
source: These data suggest that the earlier onset times for the contralateral loads were not simply due to larger changes in activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of neurons with similar magnitude differences.

claim: 53% of recorded neurons from single electrodes in Monkey P were load-sensitive.
source: We found only 53% of recorded neurons were load-sensitive, a lower percentage than we observed for the opposite hemisphere.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the percentage of load-sensitive neurons from single electrode recordings.

claim: The population response from single electrodes in Monkey P started at 35 ms for the contralateral loads and 47 ms for the ipsilateral loads.
source: The population response started at 35 ms for the contralateral loads and 47 ms for the ipsilateral loads (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement of onset times from single electrode recordings.

claim: 70% of neurons from single electrodes in Monkey P had a larger contralateral response magnitude than ipsilateral response magnitude in the perturbation epoch (median magnitude: contralateral 19.6 Hz/Nm, ipsilateral 9.2 Hz/Nm).
source: We also found the magnitude of the contralateral response was larger than the ipsilateral response for 70% of neurons in the perturbation epoch (median magnitude: contralateral 19.6 Hz/Nm, ipsilateral 9.2 Hz/Nm).

claim: During the posture epoch, ~50% of neurons from single electrodes in Monkey P had a larger contralateral response (contralateral 6.4 Hz/Nm, ipsilateral 4.1 Hz/Nm).

claim: For Monkey M, the median change in correlation coefficient between ipsilateral and contralateral loads was 0.20.

claim: The median changes in correlation coefficient were significantly larger than a null distribution generated by comparing pairwise correlations across randomly separated trials within a context (p<0.001).

claim: Ipsilateral and contralateral activity are more orthogonal than expected by random chance.

claim: For Monkey P, three ipsilateral dimensions captured 54% of the ipsilateral variance while only capturing 3% of the contralateral variance.

claim: For Monkey M, three ipsilateral dimensions captured 37% of the ipsilateral variance while only capturing 4% of the contralateral variance.
source: For Monkey p/M, we found three ipsilateral dimensions that captured 54/37% of the ipsilateral variance, while only capturing 3%/4% of the contralateral variance.

claim: The average difference between ipsilateral and contralateral activity in the ipsilateral dimensions was 116% for Monkey M, which was significant (bootstrap p<0.001).

evidence: This claim is supported by bootstrap statistical analysis of orthogonalized dimensions shown in Figure 9C.

claim: For Monkey P, three contralateral dimensions captured 62% of the contralateral variance while only capturing 3% of the ipsilateral variance.
source: Similarly, the three contralateral dimensions we found captured 62/44% of the contralateral variance for Monkey P/M, while only capturing 3%/4% of the ipsilateral variance.

claim: For Monkey M, three contralateral dimensions captured 44% of the contralateral variance while only capturing 4% of the ipsilateral variance.

claim: The average difference between contralateral and ipsilateral activity in the contralateral dimensions was 104% for Monkey M, which was significant (bootstrap p<0.001).

claim: Linearly summing each neuron's response can isolate ipsilateral neural activity from the contralateral activity, and vice versa.
source: These time-series demonstrate that linearly summing each neuron's response can isolate ipsilateral neural activity from the contralateral activity, and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the orthogonalization analysis results.

claim: ~55% of load-sensitive neurons in M1 responded to loads applied to the ipsilateral limb.
source: We found ~55% of load-sensitive neurons in M1 responded to ipsilateral and contralateral disturbances similar to reaching studies (Donchin et al., 1998; Donchin et al., 2001; Donchin et al., 2002; Donchin et al., 2002; Kermadi et al., 1998; Cardoso de Oliveira et al., 2001; Gribova et al., 2002; Cisek et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citations to similar findings in reaching studies.

claim: The fastest response to an ipsilateral load was ~10 ms after the fastest response for a contralateral load.
source: The fastest response to an ipsilateral load was ~10 ms after the fastest response for a contralateral load, suggesting the corpus callosum was relaying the ipsilateral information (Aboitiz et al., 1992; Ringo et al., 1994; Fendrich et al., 2004; Caminiti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citations to prior research on corpus callosum transmission times.

claim: The corpus callosum was relaying the ipsilateral information.
source: The fastest response to an ipsilateral load was ~10 ms after the fastest response for a contralateral load, suggesting the corpus callosum was relaying the ipsilateral information (Aboitiz et al., 1992; Ringo et al., 1994; Fendrich et al., 2004; Caminiti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing delay and citations to prior research on corpus callosum function.

claim: The delay in M1 response to ipsilateral loads matches the delay in task-dependent feedback responses between the two limbs during bimanual motor tasks.
source: This delay also matches the delay in task-dependent feedback responses between the two limbs during bimanual motor tasks (Marsden et al., 1981; Mutha and Sainburg, 2009; Dimitriou et al., 2012; Omrani et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on bimanual motor tasks.

claim: A small amount of motion in the unperturbed limb starting in <100 ms was observed following a perturbation.
source: Following a perturbation, we observed a small amount of motion in the unperturbed limb starting in <100 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic data from the current study.

claim: The small motion in the unperturbed limb may be the result of energy transferred through the trunk from the perturbed limb to the unperturbed limb.
source: This motion may be the result of energy transferred through the trunk from the perturbed limb to the unperturbed limb.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed motion.

claim: The motion in the unperturbed limb may have been generated by small muscular contractions in the unperturbed limb.
source: Alternatively, given the onset timing, the motion may have been generated by small muscular contractions in the unperturbed limb.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed motion.

claim: No changes in muscle activity in the unperturbed limb were observed.
source: However, we failed to observe any changes in muscle activity in the unperturbed limb.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data from the current study.

claim: The small motion in the unperturbed limb is an unlikely explanation for why M1 activity was observed when ipsilateral loads were applied.
source: This small motion in the unperturbed limb is an unlikely explanation for why we observed M1 activity when ipsilateral loads were applied.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from the current study.

claim: M1 responses are less sensitive to applied loads if the limb is not engaged in a task.
source: Previously, we showed M1 responses are less sensitive to applied loads if the limb is not engaged in a task (Omrani et al., 2014; Omrani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: Most M1 activity during the ipsilateral loads was likely related to the ipsilateral limb.
source: Thus, most M1 activity during the ipsilateral loads was likely related to the ipsilateral limb.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence from the current study.

claim: M1 neurons were bimodally distributed with higher proportion of neurons maximally active for combined elbow flexion and shoulder extension, and combined elbow extension and shoulder flexion.
source: Instead, M1 neurons were bimodally distributed with higher proportion of neurons maximally active for combined elbow flexion and shoulder extension, and combined elbow extension and shoulder flexion, consistent with previous studies (Cabel et al., 2001; Herter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citations to prior research.

claim: A similar distribution of preferred loads exists for proximal limb muscles.
source: A similar distribution of preferred loads exists for proximal limb muscles (Kurtzer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The bimodal distribution is opposite to the anatomical action of the bi-articular muscles, reflecting that mono-articular muscles shift their preferred load to consider loads at the non-spanned joint.
source: Notably, the bimodal distribution is opposite to the anatomical action of the bi-articular muscles, reflecting that mono-articular muscles shift their preferred load to consider loads at the non-spanned joint (Nozaki et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and represents an interpretation of the bimodal distribution.

claim: A neural network trained to control a two-joint limb displays a similar distribution in preferred loads across the network when bi-articular muscles are included.
source: A neural network trained to control a two-joint limb displays a similar distribution in preferred loads across the network when bi-articular muscles are included (Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Perturbation activity in M1 related to the ipsilateral limb reflects features related to motor output.
source: In a similar manner, perturbation activity in M1 related to the ipsilateral limb also reflects features related to motor output.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bimodal distribution of ipsilateral preferred loads.

claim: M1 activity could reliably decode ipsilateral muscle activity.
source: Recently, Ames and Churchland (2019) compared M1 responses to contralateral and ipsilateral cycling movements and found M1 activity could reliably decode ipsilateral muscle activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ames and Churchland (2019).

claim: Ipsilateral-related activity reflects the mechanical and anatomical properties of the ipsilateral limb even though the descending projections predominantly target the contralateral musculature.
source: Thus, ipsilateral-related activity is not an abstract representation of ipsilateral motor function. Rather, it reflects the mechanical and anatomical properties of the ipsilateral limb even though the descending projections predominantly target the contralateral musculature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: The present study highlights a reorganization of the population response for the ipsilateral and contralateral limbs.
source: The present study highlights a reorganization of the population response for the ipsilateral and contralateral limbs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's main finding.

claim: The preferred load was largely unrelated between the contralateral and ipsilateral limbs.
source: First, the preferred load was largely unrelated between the contralateral and ipsilateral limbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis.

claim: Preferred directions were similar for rostral areas in motor cortex between contralateral and ipsilateral reaches, whereas caudal areas exhibited little relationship.
source: They found the preferred directions were similar for rostral areas in motor cortex between contralateral and ipsilateral reaches, whereas caudal areas exhibited little relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cisek et al. (2003).

claim: For Monkey P, the recorded neurons exhibited no relationship between the preferred loads for the contralateral and ipsilateral limb.
source: For Monkey P, the recorded neurons exhibited no relationship between the preferred loads for the contralateral and ipsilateral limb, whereas for Monkey M we found a small correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis.

claim: For Monkey M, a small correlation was found between the preferred loads for the contralateral and ipsilateral limb.
source: For Monkey P, the recorded neurons exhibited no relationship between the preferred loads for the contralateral and ipsilateral limb, whereas for Monkey M we found a small correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis.

claim: Monkey M's array was placed ~2 mm more rostral than for Monkey P.
source: This may reflect that Monkey M's array was placed ~2 mm more rostral than for Monkey P (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the array placement.

claim: Applying the same weights used to construct population vectors from contralateral reaches to the ipsilateral activity would result in negligible vector magnitudes.
source: Relatedly, Steinberg et al. (2002) constructed population vectors (PV) from M1 activity during contralateral reaches by linearly weighting each neuron's response. Applying the same weights to the ipsilateral activity found vector magnitudes that were negligible.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steinberg et al. (2002).

claim: A similar reduction in PV magnitude would likely be observed in the current study given the substantial change in tuning.
source: It seems likely we would have observed a similar reduction in PV magnitude given the substantial change in tuning, although the bimodal distribution of preferred-loads would have a complex effect on PV direction and magnitude (Scott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: M1 activity related to the two limbs was not simply random or uncorrelated.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate a mechanism by which ipsilateral activity in M1 does not lead to contralateral motor output. We found M1 activity related to the two limbs was not simply random or uncorrelated.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis.

claim: Ipsilateral activity was specifically organized into a subspace that was almost orthogonal to the subspace of the contralateral limb.
source: Rather, ipsilateral activity was specifically organized into a subspace that was almost orthogonal to the subspace of the contralateral limb, similar to Ames and Churchland (2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis and a citation to similar findings.

claim: The contralateral activity can be isolated from the ipsilateral activity simply by summing a linear weighting of each neuron's response.
source: This allowed us to isolate the contralateral activity from the ipsilateral activity simply by summing a linear weighting of each neuron's response (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data analysis and citations to prior methods.

claim: The synaptic weights of M1 neurons that project onto spinal circuits could be assigned such that the net effect of ipsilateral activity cancels out.
source: This may provide a mechanism for how ipsilateral activity does not generate motor output. Thus, the synaptic weights of M1 neurons that project onto spinal circuits could be assigned such that the net effect of ipsilateral activity cancels out.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the orthogonality findings.

claim: One could not infer that contralateral and ipsilateral activity reside in orthogonal subspaces based solely on the change in preferred load direction.
source: However, it is important to note that one could not infer that contralateral and ipsilateral activity reside in orthogonal subspaces based solely on the change in preferred load direction (Kaufman et al., 2014; Elsayed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological point supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Temporal dynamics can arise on time scales shorter than the epoch used to assess the preferred load thus contributing little to a neuron's preferred load.
source: These temporal dynamics can arise on time scales shorter than the epoch used to assess the preferred load thus contributing little to a neuron's preferred load (ex. Figure 9A projection three contralateral activity).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by example data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: If temporal dynamics dominate the variance of a neuron's firing rate, then one can have a substantial change in preferred loads without a substantial change in the subspace the population resides in.
source: If these temporal dynamics dominate the variance of a neuron's firing rate, than one can have a substantial change in preferred loads without a substantial change in the subspace the population resides in.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the nature of temporal dynamics and subspace analysis.

claim: Both analyses (preferred load and subspace) provide complementary evidence for a network reorganization for representing the contralateral and ipsilateral limb.
source: Both analyses provide complementary evidence for a network reorganization for representing the contralateral and ipsilateral limb.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the complementary nature of the analyses.

claim: The subspaces related to the contralateral limb may not be fixed.
source: It is interesting to note that the subspaces related to the contralateral limb may not be fixed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement introducing discussion of subspace flexibility.

claim: M1 activity remains in the same subspace during motor learning.
source: M1 activity remains in the same subspace during motor learning (Golub et al., 2018; Perich et al., 2018; Vyas et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M1 activity remains in the same subspace during reaching tasks with different load conditions.
source: and during reaching tasks with different load conditions (Gribble and Scott, 2002; Gallego et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M1 activity remains in the same subspace during reaching tasks with different initiation cues.
source: and initiation cues (Lara et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Activity during locomotion and reaching occupied orthogonal subspaces that may allow motor cortex to engage separate spinal circuits for each behavior.
source: However, Miri et al. (2017) demonstrated that activity during locomotion and reaching occupied orthogonal subspaces that may allow motor cortex to engage separate spinal circuits for each behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miri et al. (2017).

claim: A similar mechanism for engaging spinal circuits may exist for load-related activity during posture and reaching.
source: A similar mechanism for engaging spinal circuits may exist for load-related activity during posture and reaching.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: A neuron's gain during posture showed no relationship with its gain during reaching.
source: Previously, we found a neuron's gain during posture showed no relationship with its gain during reaching (Kurtzer et al., 2005), which may reflect neural activity in separate subspaces for these motor actions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Different classes of behavior (posture versus movement versus locomotion) have distinct subspaces.
source: This suggests that different classes of behavior, posture versus movement versus locomotion, have distinct subspaces.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current study's findings and prior research.

claim: Distinct subspaces for different behaviors may reflect differences in control policies for each behavior, and how motor responses to sensory feedback must be modified across these behaviours.
source: This may reflect differences in control policies for each behavior, and how motor responses to sensory feedback must be modified across these behavours (Todorov and Jordan, 2002; Scott, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Brain regions that utilize the ipsilateral activity can weight each neuron's response to extract the ipsilateral activity without interference from the contralateral activity.
source: Brain regions that utilize the ipsilateral activity can also weight each neuron's response to extract the ipsilateral activity without interference from the contralateral activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the orthogonality of ipsilateral and contralateral subspaces.

claim: Activity in ipsilateral motor cortex improves the robustness of activity in the contralateral motor cortex.
source: Li et al. (2016) highlights how activity in ipsilateral motor cortex improves the robustness of activity in the contralateral motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al. (2016).

claim: The ipsilateral subspace may allow for flexible bimanual coupling when both limbs are utilized for a bimanual task.
source: The ipsilateral subspace may also allow for flexible bimanual coupling when both limbs are utilized for a bimanual task (Marsden et al., 1981; Diedrichsen, 2007; Mutha and Sainburg, 2009; Dimitriou et al., 2012; Omrani et al., 2013; Córdova Bulens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to prior research on bimanual tasks.

claim: The ipsilateral subspace may be altered following spinal cord injuries or stroke to allow ipsilateral M1 to contribute to descending motor output.
source: In addition, this subspace may be altered following spinal cord injuries or stroke to allow ipsilateral M1 to contribute to descending motor output (Cramer et al., 1997; Nishimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to prior research on neural plasticity after injury.

claim: The ability to isolate neural activity in subspaces that do not influence spinal circuits has implications for a long-standing debate regarding M1's involvement in descending control.
source: The ability to isolate neural activity in subspaces that do not influence spinal circuits has implications for a long-standing debate regarding M1's involvement in descending control.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Many studies have found M1 activity correlates with muscle activity.
source: Many studies have found M1 activity correlates with muscle activity (Evarts, 1968; Humphrey, 1972; Murphy et al., 1985; Bennett and Lemon, 1996; Scott, 1997; Sergio and Kalaska, 1998; Kakei et al., 1999; Cherian et al., 2013; Oby et al., 2013; Heming et al., 2016), suggesting that M1 activity reflects low-level features of the motor output.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Other studies have correlated M1 activity with whole limb movements.
source: However, other studies have correlated M1 activity with whole limb movements (Georgopoulos et al., 1982)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Other studies have correlated M1 activity with trajectories.
source: trajectories (Schwartz, 1992; Schwartz, 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Other studies have correlated M1 activity with other high level parameters of motion.
source: and other high level parameters of motion (Johnson et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When high and low-level features of motor action are dissociated, some M1 activity still appears to be related to high level features of the movement.
source: Even when high and low-level features of motor action are dissociated, some activity still appears to be related to high level features of the movement (Thach, 1978; Sergio and Kalaska, 1998; Kakei et al., 1999; Russo et al., 2018).

claim: Both high-level and low-level information could be present in M1 simultaneously, but only low-level motor commands influence spinal circuits.
source: Our data suggest that both sets of information could be present in M1 simultaneously, but only low-level motor commands influence spinal circuits (Lalazar et al., 2019).

claim: By retaining different types and sources of information in different subspaces, neural activity can both control motor output and process other types of information simultaneously.
source: By retaining different types and sources of information in different subspaces, neural activity can both control motor output and process other types of information simultaneously whether it is related to high level features of movement or even the ipsilateral limb.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the current study's findings.

claim: Two non-human primates (Macaca mulatta) were used in the studies.

claim: Studies were approved by the Queen's University Research Ethics Board and Animal Care Committee.
source: Studies were approved by the Queen's University Research Ethics Board and Animal Care Committee.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

source: The animals performed a postural perturbation task similar to our previous studies (Herter et al., 2009; Pruszynski et al., 2014).

claim: Eight load conditions were used for each limb, consisting of torques that caused elbow flexion, elbow extension, shoulder flexion or shoulder extension, or the four multi-joint combinations of torques.
source: Eight load conditions were used for each limb, consisting of torques that caused elbow flexion (EF), elbow extension (EE), shoulder flexion (SF) or shoulder extension (SE), or the four multi-joint combinations of torques (SF/EF, SF/EE, SE/EF, SE/EE, Figure 10B).

evidence: This is a direct statement about the neural recording method.

claim: Spike waveforms were sampled at 30 kHz.
source: Spike waveforms were sampled at 30 kHz and acquired using a 128-Channel Neural Signal Processor (Blackrock Microsystems, Salt Lake City, UT).

claim: For Monkey P, neurons were recorded from three behavioral sessions spaced 4 months apart.
source: For Monkey P's array, we recorded neurons from three behavioral sessions spaced 4 months apart.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recording timeline.

claim: For Monkey M, neurons were recorded from three behavioral sessions, with over a year between the first and second session, and three months between the second and third session.
source: For Monkey M, we also collected from three behavioral sessions, with over a year between the first and second session, and three months between the second and third session.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recording timeline.

claim: Only well isolated single units were used for analysis and no outliers were removed.
source: Only well isolated single units were used for analysis and no outliers were removed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data inclusion criteria.

claim: Previous studies estimate that 10–50% of neurons can be reliably tracked over a two-week period.
source: Previous studies estimate that 10–50% of neurons can be reliably tracked over a two-week period (Jackson and Fetz, 2007; Tolias et al., 2007; Dickey et al., 2009; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Virtually no neurons could be reliably tracked over 100 days.
source: Furthermore, Fraser and Schwartz (2012) tracked neurons over the course of 100 days and found that virtually no neurons could be reliably tracked over this extended time period.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fraser and Schwartz (2012).

claim: The number of reliably-tracked neurons appears to decay exponentially over time.
source: The number of reliably-tracked neurons also appears to decay exponentially over time (Tolias et al., 2007; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012).
